articles.body_html:
AI agents are easy to demo when they follow a clean path: receive a task, call a tool, produce an answer, and finish successfully.

They become much harder to reason about when multiple agents run together.

In a real system, agents may plan, call tools, retry failures, make decisions from stale state, run in parallel, or touch the same resource from different paths. When something breaks, flat logs usually tell us what happened, but they rarely show why it happened.

That is the debugging gap I wanted to explore.

So I built a small TypeScript-based multi-agent incident-response simulator. The goal was simple: simulate a production incident where multiple agents diagnose and remediate infrastructure problems. The system had a diagnostic agent, database agent, network agent, scaling agent, and coordinator agent.

On paper, the design looked reasonable.

The DiagnosticAgent analyzed the incoming incident. The DatabaseAgent handled database-related issues. The NetworkAgent managed load balancer or routing problems. The ScalingAgent handled capacity decisions. The CoordinatorAgent orchestrated everything and was responsible for avoiding conflicting actions.

The architecture looked clean until the agents started working at the same time.

The Problem With Flat Logs

In the first version, the simulator emitted logs like this:

\[2:47:23\] DiagnosticAgent: High DB latency detected  
\[2:47:24\] DatabaseAgent: Initiating replica scale-up  
\[2:47:25\] DiagnosticAgent: Connection pool exhaustion detected  
\[2:47:26\] DatabaseAgent: Taking node-3 offline for maintenance  
\[2:47:27\] ScalingAgent: Database performance degraded, scaling up  
\[2:47:28\] NetworkAgent: Detected backend failures, restarting load balancer  
\[2:47:29\] CoordinatorAgent: Conflict detected  
\[2:47:32\] ERROR: Cluster quorum lost

These logs were useful, but only up to a point.

They showed that the database agent scaled replicas. They showed that another agent also tried to scale. They showed that a node was taken offline. They showed that the coordinator noticed a conflict.

But they did not clearly answer the important questions:

Which agent made a decision from stale state?

Did the coordinator run before or after the conflicting tool calls?

Were the database and scaling agents truly running in parallel?

Which exact tool call caused the final failure?

Was the problem an LLM decision, a tool execution issue, or a coordination issue?

This is where normal logging started to feel too flat. The system behavior was no longer a simple list of events. It was a tree of decisions, tool calls, retries, and parallel branches.

That is when I tried agent-inspect.

Adding Local Execution Tracing

agent-inspect is a local-first execution tree debugger for TypeScript and Node.js AI agents. Instead of sending traces to a hosted dashboard, it writes local traces that can be inspected from the terminal.

That local-first model is important during development. I did not want to set up a full observability platform just to understand one local agent run. I wanted something closer to a structured debugging layer between console.log and production-grade observability.

The first step was to wrap the coordinator flow.

import { inspectRun, step } from "agent-inspect";

async function handleIncident(incident: Incident) {  
 return inspectRun(  
   "incident-response-coordinator",  
   async () \=\> {  
     const diagnosis \= await step("diagnose-incident", async () \=\> {  
       return diagnosticAgent.analyze(incident);  
     });

     const actions \= await step("execute-remediation", async () \=\> {  
       return Promise.all(\[  
         step.tool("database-remediation", () \=\>  
           databaseAgent.handleIssue(diagnosis.dbIssues)  
         ),  
         step.tool("network-remediation", () \=\>  
           networkAgent.handleIssue(diagnosis.networkIssues)  
         ),  
         step.tool("scaling-remediation", () \=\>  
           scalingAgent.handleIssue(diagnosis.scalingIssues)  
         ),  
       \]);  
     });

     return step("resolve-conflicts", async () \=\> {  
       return resolveConflicts(actions);  
     });  
   },  
   {  
     traceDir: "./.agent-inspect",  
   }  
 );  
}

The code did not need a full rewrite. The main change was adding meaningful boundaries around the work.

The outer inspectRun represented one agent run. The normal step calls represented logical phases. The step.tool calls marked operations that touched external systems or simulated infrastructure.

Then I instrumented the database agent.

class DatabaseAgent {  
 async handleIssue(issues: DbIssue\[\]) {  
   return step("database-agent-execution", async () \=\> {  
     const dbState \= await step.tool("check-db-state", async () \=\> {  
       return this.getClusterState();  
     });

     const decision \= await step.llm("decide-db-action", async () \=\> {  
       return this.llm.chat({  
         messages: \[  
           {  
             role: "user",  
             content: JSON.stringify({  
               task: "Decide the safest database remediation action",  
               issues,  
               dbState,  
             }),  
           },  
         \],  
       });  
     });

     if (decision.action \=== "scale-up") {  
       return step.tool("scale-database", async () \=\> {  
         return this.scaleUpReplicas(decision.targetCount);  
       });  
     }

     if (decision.action \=== "restart-node") {  
       return step.tool("restart-node", async () \=\> {  
         return this.restartNode(decision.nodeId);  
       });  
     }

     return {  
       action: "no-op",  
       reason: "No safe database action selected",  
     };  
   });  
 }  
}

The important part is not just the tracing. It is the naming.

A trace is only useful if the steps describe the system in the same language engineers use during debugging. check-db-state, decide-db-action, scale-database, and restart-node are much more useful than generic messages like running task or tool call started.

Inspecting the Failed Run

After running the simulator, I listed the local traces:

npx agent-inspect list --dir ./.agent-inspect

Then I inspected the failed run:

npx agent-inspect view <run-id> --dir ./.agent-inspect

The execution tree made the issue much easier to understand:

incident-response-coordinator                              \[47.2s\] ✗  
├─ diagnose-incident                                       \[3.1s\] ✓  
├─ execute-remediation                                     \[41.8s\] ✗  
│  ├─ database-remediation                                 \[23.2s\] ✓  
│  │  └─ database-agent-execution                          \[23.1s\] ✓  
│  │     ├─ check-db-state                                 \[0.4s\] ✓  
│  │     ├─ decide-db-action                               \[2.1s\] ✓  
│  │     ├─ scale-database                                 \[18.3s\] ✓  
│  │     ├─ check-db-state                                 \[0.3s\] ✓  
│  │     ├─ decide-db-action                               \[1.9s\] ✓  
│  │     └─ restart-node                                   \[0.3s\] ✓  
│  ├─ network-remediation                                  \[5.2s\] ✓  
│  └─ scaling-remediation                                  \[41.7s\] ✗  
│     └─ scaling-agent-execution                           \[41.6s\] ✗  
│        ├─ check-scaling-state                            \[0.3s\] ✓  
│        ├─ decide-scaling-action                          \[2.2s\] ✓  
│        └─ scale-database                                 \[39.1s\] ✗  
│           └─ Error: Operation timeout \- cluster in inconsistent state  
└─ resolve-conflicts                                       \[not reached\]

This view showed the problem more clearly than the logs.

The database agent checked the state, decided to scale up, and started a database scaling operation. Then it checked state again and decided to restart a node. At the same time, the scaling agent also detected database pressure and started another scaling operation.

Both agents were acting on the same resource. Both believed their action was valid. The coordinator was supposed to resolve conflicts, but the trace showed that resolve-conflicts was never reached because the failure happened inside the parallel remediation step.

That was the real bug.

It was not simply a bad prompt. It was not only a database operation failure. It was a coordination bug caused by parallel agents acting on the same resource without a proper resource-level guard.

Fixing the Coordination Model

Once the execution tree made the failure visible, the fix became much more direct.

The first change was to add a state refresh guard. If the database cluster already had an operation in progress, the agent should wait for stable state before making another decision.

async function handleIssue(issues: DbIssue\[\]) {  
 return step("database-agent-execution", async () \=\> {  
   const dbState \= await step.tool("check-db-state", async () \=\> {  
     return this.getClusterState();  
   });

   if (dbState.hasInProgressOperations) {  
     return step("wait-for-stability", async () \=\> {  
       await this.waitForStableState();  
       return this.handleIssue(issues);  
     });  
   }

   return this.decideAndExecute(issues, dbState);  
 });  
}

The second change was to protect critical operations with a lock.

async function scaleUpReplicas(targetCount: number) {  
 return step.tool("scale-database", async () \=\> {  
   const lock \= await this.acquireLock("database-scaling", 60\_000);

   try {  
     return this.performScaleUp(targetCount);  
   } finally {  
     await lock.release();  
   }  
 });  
}

The third change was at the coordinator level. If multiple agents wanted to touch the same resource, the coordinator should not blindly run them in parallel.

const actions \= await step("execute-remediation-sequenced", async () \=\> {  
 const targets \= identifyResourceTargets(diagnosis);

 if (targets.database.length \> 0\) {  
   const dbActions \= await step.tool("database-remediation", () \=\>  
     databaseAgent.handleIssue(diagnosis.dbIssues)  
   );

   const networkActions \= await step.tool("network-remediation", () \=\>  
     networkAgent.handleIssue(diagnosis.networkIssues)  
   );

   return {  
     dbActions,  
     networkActions,  
   };  
 }

 return Promise.all(\[  
   step.tool("network-remediation", () \=\>  
     networkAgent.handleIssue(diagnosis.networkIssues)  
   ),  
   step.tool("scaling-remediation", () \=\>  
     scalingAgent.handleIssue(diagnosis.scalingIssues)  
   ),  
 \]);  
});

After the fix, the trace looked different:

incident-response-coordinator                              \[15.3s\] ✓  
├─ diagnose-incident                                       \[2.8s\] ✓  
├─ execute-remediation-sequenced                           \[11.2s\] ✓  
│  └─ database-remediation                                 \[8.4s\] ✓  
│     └─ database-agent-execution                          \[8.3s\] ✓  
│        ├─ check-db-state                                 \[0.3s\] ✓  
│        ├─ acquire-lock                                   \[0.1s\] ✓  
│        ├─ decide-db-action                               \[1.9s\] ✓  
│        ├─ scale-database                                 \[5.8s\] ✓  
│        └─ release-lock                                   \[0.1s\] ✓  
└─ resolve-conflicts                                       \[1.3s\] ✓

This is the kind of output I want during agent development.

Not just “something failed,” but where it failed. Not just “the tool timed out,” but what sequence caused the timeout. Not just “agents ran in parallel,” but which branches actually overlapped.

Why This Matters for AI Agent Engineering

As agent systems become more common, debugging needs to move beyond raw logs.

A single-agent workflow can often be debugged with a few log statements. But multi-agent systems introduce coordination problems. A bug may not live inside one function. It may live between two valid decisions that become unsafe when executed together.

That is why execution trees are useful.

They show the structure of the run. They show parent-child relationships. They separate normal logic from tool calls and LLM calls. They make retries, skipped steps, failed branches, and slow operations easier to reason about.

This also changes how we think about observability.

Production observability platforms are still important. Tools like LangSmith, Langfuse, OpenTelemetry-based pipelines, and APM platforms solve important team and production problems. But during local development, I often want something lighter. I want to run the agent, inspect the trace, make a change, and compare the result.

That is the space where a local-first tool like agent-inspect fits naturally.

It is not trying to replace production monitoring. It is closer to a developer workflow tool for understanding agent behavior before it reaches production.

Practical Lessons From the Project

The first lesson is that flat logs hide structure. In a multi-agent workflow, order alone is not enough. You need to know which step belonged to which agent, which steps were siblings, and which operation blocked or failed.

The second lesson is that not every agent bug is an LLM bug. In this simulator, the expensive failure came from tool coordination and stale state, not from a slow model call. Without tracing, it would have been easy to spend time tuning prompts while ignoring the actual failure path.

The third lesson is that instrumentation can become living documentation. A well-named step() call describes the architecture. When a new engineer reads the trace, they can understand the runtime behavior faster than reading scattered logs.

The fourth lesson is that local-first debugging is still valuable. Not every debugging session needs a dashboard, collector, account, or cloud upload. Sometimes the fastest path is a local trace file and a terminal command.

Final Thoughts

The more I build with AI agents, the more I feel that debugging is becoming an architecture problem.

It is not enough to know that an agent produced the wrong answer. We need to know what it planned, which tools it called, which state it observed, which branches ran in parallel, where retries happened, and what changed between two runs.

For TypeScript and Node.js teams building agentic systems, agent-inspect is a useful tool to explore that workflow. It gives you a lightweight way to turn agent runs into readable execution trees without committing to a hosted observability setup on day one.

For my multi-agent incident-response simulator, the biggest value was simple: it turned a confusing wall of logs into a system I could reason about.

And that is usually the first step toward making agent systems reliable.

Npm lib: https://www.npmjs.com/package/agent-inspect

Github repo: https://github.com/rajudandigam/agent-inspect

articles.title: The Scheduling Boundaries Behind Responsive UI
articles.description: This is the last article in a series on how JavaScript actually runs. You can read the full series...
articles.body_html:
This is the last article in a series on how JavaScript actually runs. You can read the full series here or on my website.

We now know how the event loop and rendering pipeline behave.

The browser:

  • Runs a macrotask to completion.
  • Drains all microtasks.
  • Executes any scheduled requestAnimationFrame callbacks.
  • Drains all microtasks.
  • Performs layout and paint to produce the next frame.
  • Moves on to the next macrotask.

Given that environment, how should we write UI code?

Long Tasks Block Everything

If you want the UI to stay responsive, your tasks must yield quickly.

Consider this:

button.addEventListener("click", () => {
  const start = performance.now();

  while (performance.now() - start < 3000) {
    // busy loop for 3 seconds
  }

  console.log("done");
});

Once the button is clicked, the page becomes unresponsive. The click handler is a macrotask and nothing can interrupt it. Everything else has to wait: there is no re-rendering, no new input, no requestAnimationFrame callbacks.

Long-running tasks monopolize the main thread. While they run, rendering pauses, input waits, animations stall and timers are delayed. Responsive UI depends on cooperation.

Microtasks Do Not Yield to Rendering

Chaining promises look like a way to break work into pieces:

button.addEventListener("click", () => {
  Promise.resolve()
    .then(() => heavyWork())
    .then(() => {
      status.textContent = "Halfway...";
    })
    .then(() => moreHeavyWork())
    .then(() => {
      status.textContent = "Done";
    });
});

However, each .then() callback becomes a microtask when its associated Promise resolves. Because the browser must drain the entire microtask queue before rendering, chaining Promises does not create render opportunities. As a result, the user sees nothing until "Done" shows up on screen.

If you want to let the browser render, you must introduce a scheduling boundary:

button.addEventListener("click", () => {
  Promise.resolve()
    .then(() => heavyWork())
    .then(() => {
      status.textContent = "Halfway...";

      return new Promise(resolve => {
        // setTimeout used to introduce a scheduling boundary
        setTimeout(resolve, 0); 
      });
    })
    .then(() => heavyWork())
    .then(() => {
      status.textContent = "Done";
    });
});

Alternatively, we can consider:

button.addEventListener("click", () => {
  Promise.resolve()
    .then(() => heavyWork()
    .then(() => {
      status.textContent = "Halfway...";

      return new Promise(resolve => {
        // requestAnimationFrame used to introduce a scheduling boundary
        requestAnimationFrame(resolve); 
      });
    })
    .then(() => heavyWork()
    .then(() => {
      status.textContent = "Done";
    });
});

Both approaches work because a .then() callback is only queued once its associated Promise resolves. By returning a Promise that resolves later, we delay when the next microtask is created. setTimeout yields to the next macrotask, while requestAnimationFrame yields to the next frame.

Choosing Between Promises, setTimeout and requestAnimationFrame

These mechanisms signal different intentions to the browser. They are not interchangeable.

Use a Promise when you need to continue work immediately after the current macrotask completes, but before the browser moves on. They are ideal for continuing work that logically depends on previous work. They help to preserve order, transform results and update state after completion. They are not a yielding mechanism.

Use setTimeout when you need to create a real scheduling gap. They are useful for breaking up long computation, deferring non-critical work and yielding cooperatively. They are general purpose yields.

Use requestAnimationFrame when you are performing visual updates. It is ideal for animations and layout-sensitive work.

Align Visual Updates to Frames

Consider this approach:

document.addEventListener("mousemove", (event) => {
  box.style.left = event.clientX + "px";
});

If the mouse fires 200 events per second, this code attempts 200 DOM updates per second. But on most displays, the refresh happens about 60 times per second. Visual work that exceeds that rate is simply wasted.

Instead, consider:

let latestX = 0;
let scheduled = false;

document.addEventListener("mousemove", (event) => {
  latestX = event.clientX;

  if (!scheduled) {
    scheduled = true;

    requestAnimationFrame(() => {
      box.style.left = latestX + "px";
      scheduled = false;
    });
  }
});

We use requestAnimationFrame to update at most once per frame, no matter the rate at which input can fire.

Respect the Frame Budget

requestAnimationFrame guarantees alignment to the frames but it does not guarantee smoothness. On a 60fps display, the browser has roughly 16ms per frames. That 16ms must include all JavaScript and rendering work.

If the JavaScript executed alone takes longer than that, the browser cannot complete rendering in time:

requestAnimationFrame(() => {
  const start = performance.now();

  while (performance.now() - start < 40) {
    // 40ms of work
  }
});

This callback runs before the browser renders but it blocks for 40ms and therefore exceeds the frame budget. Since the browser cannot display partial frames, if the 16ms window is missed, that frame is dropped. Instead of rendering at 60 frames per second, the browser renders less frequently: Animations can appear jerky, motion uneven and interactions delayed.

So while requestAnimationFrame helped with alignment, we must still finish the frame work within the frame window. Either work fits inside the budget or it is spread across multiple frames. For instance, this could mean animating in steps or deferring non-critical computation.

Responsive UI requires both correct scheduling and work that fits inside the budget.

Guard Against Stale Asynchronous Work

Asynchronous code creates delays. During this window, state can change:

function loadData() {
  fetch("/data")
    .then(response => response.json())
    .then(data => {
      render(data);
    });
}

This looks harmless but imagine the user clicking twice quickly and loadData() is called twice in succession. If the second request finishes first, the first request would render stale data and the UI would then be incorrect.

One common pattern is to guard against outdated work:

let currentRequestId = 0;

function loadData() {
  const id = ++currentRequestId;

  fetch("/data")
    .then(response => response.json())
    .then(data => {
      if (id !== currentRequestId) return;
      render(data);
    });
}

Now each request captures its own response and only the most recent request is allowed to update the UI.

Designing With the Browser, Not Against It

Responsive UI emerges from working within the browser's execution model.

In practice, that often means:

  • Keeping tasks short so the browser can continue scheduling
  • Remembering that microtasks do not yield to rendering
  • Aligning visual updates to frame boundaries
  • Ensuring that work fits within the frame budget.
  • Verifying that delayed work is still relevant before applying it

I started this series because I had code that used Promises, setTimeout, and requestAnimationFrame. They all felt “asynchronous” and interchangeable. Turns out they weren't.

Good UI code knows which scheduling boundary to use and when.

This article was originally published on my website.

articles.title: I Rebuilt My Next.js Starter From Scratch on Next 16 — Here's Every Decision I Made (and Why)
articles.description: I Rebuilt My Next.js Starter From Scratch on Next 16 — Here's Every Decision I Made (and...
articles.body_html:
I Rebuilt My Next.js Starter From Scratch on Next 16 — Here's Every Decision I Made (and Why)

TL;DR — I rebuilt my Next.js starter on Next 16 + React 19 with one rule: every default should be the one I'd pick on day 90, not day 1. The result has dual HTTP clients (fetch + axios) on a shared foundation with a universal/server entry split, a typed Socket.IO layer with a hard SSR boundary, a per-request Redux store that hydrates from Server Components, zod-validated env that fails fast, Biome instead of ESLint + Prettier, and a 'use client' regression sentinel that fails the build if next/headers ever leaks into the client bundle. This article walks through every load-bearing decision and the trap each one avoids.

If you've been doing Next.js for a while, you know the feeling. You spin up create-next-app, and within a week you've added the same eight things you always add: a logger, env validation, an HTTP client that doesn't throw, a state store, i18n, a theme provider, secure storage, and a CI pipeline. Then the project ships, six months pass, and you discover the HTTP client silently broke when you moved a component to a Server Component. Or your env vars failed validation at runtime instead of at boot. Or your Redux store gave the same instance to two concurrent requests in SSR.

I rebuilt my starter from scratch on Next.js 16 with one goal: bake the day-90 defaults into day 1. This isn't a "10 must-have Next.js libraries" listicle. It's the design rationale for every load-bearing choice — and the specific trap each choice avoids.

The code is at github.com/teispace/nextjs-starter. The package lives at @teispace/next-themes for the theme story; the starter itself is a template. A separate CLI (@teispace/next-maker) scaffolds applications from it.

Table of contents

  1. The "not the Next.js you know" preamble
  2. Why Biome replaced ESLint + Prettier
  3. Env validation: zod, cached, fail-fast
  4. The HTTP layer: the hardest decision in the repo
  5. The build-time tripwire that catches the bug you can't reproduce
  6. Either + ApiException: errors as values
  7. The WebSocket layer: same pattern, stricter rules
  8. Per-request Redux store with SSR-safe persistence
  9. i18n with next-intl: static rendering that actually works
  10. Logger, secure storage, and the small things that compound
  11. Quality gates: three Husky hooks, one CI workflow, a custom deprecated-API scanner
  12. What I deliberately left out
  13. Lessons that generalize beyond this starter

1. The "not the Next.js you know" preamble

The first line of the project's AGENTS.md is a warning:

This version has breaking changes — APIs, conventions, and file structure may all differ from your training data. Read the relevant guide in node_modules/next/dist/docs/ before writing any code. Heed deprecation notices.

Two things changed in Next 16 that bite anyone whose mental model was set in 13/14/15:

middleware.ts is gone. It's proxy.ts now. Same idea — edge interception of requests — but the file name, the exported function name, and the matcher syntax all changed. If you blindly copy the middleware from your last project, the build silently won't pick it up.

// src/proxy.ts
import type { NextRequest } from 'next/server';
import createMiddleware from 'next-intl/middleware';

import { routing } from './i18n/routing';

export function proxy(request: NextRequest) {
  const handleI18nRouting = createMiddleware(routing);
  return handleI18nRouting(request);
}

export const config = {
  matcher: [
    '/((?!api|trpc|_next/static|_next/image|_vercel|favicon.ico|robots.txt|sitemap.xml|manifest.webmanifest|sw.js|opengraph-image\\.[^/]+|twitter-image\\.[^/]+|apple-icon\\.[^/]+|icon\\.[^/]+|.*\\.(?:js|css|map|json|svg|png|jpg|jpeg|gif|webp|avif|ico|woff|woff2|ttf|otf|eot|mp4|webm)).*)',
  ],
};

That matcher looks ugly because it has to be: it excludes API routes, Next internals, every public/static asset Next emits, and every common static extension. Get any of those wrong and you'll see the locale-routing middleware trying to handle requests for favicon.ico or og-image.png. Painful to debug, trivial to copy-paste.

React Compiler is on by default in the config. next.config.ts enables reactCompiler: true. Most code is unaffected; code that depended on referential stability of inline callbacks (e.g. memoization tricks that relied on the same function identity across renders) may behave differently. Worth knowing before you blame your useEffect.

3. Env validation: zod, cached, fail-fast

The default Next.js story for environment variables is process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_FOO. The typings say string | undefined. So every read is either a non-null assertion (which lies) or a runtime check (which propagates everywhere).

The starter inverts this. There's exactly one place env vars are read, and they're validated against a zod schema at module load.

// src/lib/env/schema.ts
import { z } from 'zod';

export const emptyStringToUndefined = (value: unknown): unknown =>
  typeof value === 'string' && value.trim() === '' ? undefined : value;

export const envSchema = z.object({
  NODE_ENV: z.enum(['development', 'test', 'production']).default('development'),

  NEXT_PUBLIC_API_URL: z
    .preprocess(emptyStringToUndefined, z.url().optional())
    .describe('Bare origin of the backing API. The /api/v{n} prefix is appended internally.'),

  NEXT_PUBLIC_APP_URL: z
    .preprocess(emptyStringToUndefined, z.url().default('http://localhost:3000')),

  DEFAULT_TIMEZONE: z
    .preprocess(emptyStringToUndefined, z.string().default('UTC')),

  DEFAULT_LOCALE: z
    .preprocess(emptyStringToUndefined, z.string().default('en')),
});

export type Env = z.infer<typeof envSchema>;

// src/lib/env/index.ts
let cached: Env | null = null;

function readRawEnv(): Record<string, unknown> {
  return {
    NODE_ENV: process.env.NODE_ENV,
    NEXT_PUBLIC_API_URL: process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_API_URL,
    NEXT_PUBLIC_APP_URL: process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_APP_URL,
    DEFAULT_TIMEZONE: process.env.DEFAULT_TIMEZONE,
    DEFAULT_LOCALE: process.env.DEFAULT_LOCALE,
  };
}

export const env: Env = (() => {
  if (!cached) cached = validateConfig(envSchema, readRawEnv(), 'environment variables');
  return cached;
})();

The trick is the emptyStringToUndefined preprocessor. .env files have a nasty quirk: FOO= parses as the empty string "", not undefined. If you write z.string().default('UTC'), the default fires only on undefined — the empty string sails through and breaks downstream. The preprocessor normalizes empty/whitespace-only strings to undefined so defaults work the way humans expect.

The shared validator throws with a formatted multi-bullet error:

// src/lib/env/validate.ts
export function validateConfig<T>(schema, config, label = 'environment variables'): T {
  const parsed = schema.safeParse(config);
  if (!parsed.success) {
    throw new Error(
      `Invalid ${label}:\n${formatIssues(parsed.error.issues)}\n\n` +
        `Fix .env (or the relevant source) and retry.`,
    );
  }
  return parsed.data;
}

What this gets you in practice: a misconfigured deploy fails on the very first request with a readable error listing every invalid field. No more "the page is blank and the console says Cannot read properties of undefined."

There's a small companion script (scripts/sync-env.ts) wired into the pre-commit hook. It reads your .env and writes a sanitized .env.example — preserving keys and structure but stripping values from non-public entries. Lines tagged with # -public keep their values; everything else is reduced to KEY=. The pre-commit hook runs yarn env:sync --check and fails if the two are out of sync, so contributors can't accidentally commit a secret to .env.example.

NEXT_PUBLIC_API_URL=
NEXT_PUBLIC_APP_URL=

DEFAULT_TIMEZONE=
DEFAULT_LOCALE=

PORT=3000 # -public

CONTAINER_NAME=next-app # -public
IMAGE_NAME=nextjs-starter # -public
IMAGE_TAG=latest # -public

The convention: when you add a new env var, you touch three places — schema.ts, readRawEnv() in index.ts, and .env.example. The pre-commit hook catches the third one if you forget.

4. The HTTP layer: the hardest decision in the repo

This is the piece I spent the most time on, broke twice, and finally got right on the third design. I'll spare you the dead ends and just describe the live design.

The contract

Every HTTP call returns ResultAsync<T> = Promise<Either<ApiException, T>> and never throws. Network errors, 5xx, 4xx, validation errors — everything lands on the left side of an Either. You destructure it at the call site:

import { fetchClient } from '@/lib/utils/http';

const result = await fetchClient.get<User>('/users/123');

if (result.isLeft()) {
  // result.value is an ApiException — typed
  return showError(result.value);
}

const user = result.value; // typed as User

Why "never throws"? Because every team I've worked on eventually ends up with try/catch boilerplate around every API call, and half of those try/catches leak (someone forgets one, the exception bubbles up to a generic error boundary, and you lose the field-level validation errors the API returned). Making the failure visible in the type signature forces the call site to deal with it — and once you've done that, the boilerplate disappears.

Two clients, same surface

The starter ships both a fetchClient and an axiosClient. Same method signatures, same return type, same options shape. Why both?

  • fetchClient is the default. Zero KB on top of the native Fetch API, works in the Edge runtime, RSC, Server Actions, Route Handlers, and the browser. This is what you should reach for first.
  • axiosClient is there for the cases where you actually need axios features — request cancellation tokens, advanced transforms, or just because a third-party SDK expects an axios interceptor. About 30 KB of bundle. Not available in the Edge runtime.

Both clients pass through the same shared/ foundation: the same request-ID generator, the same parseApiError pipeline, the same toSearchParams serializer. The point of having both is that you can mix runtimes without rewriting your call sites — and you can swap one for the other without changing anything except the import.

The universal/server split (this is the load-bearing bit)

Cookie-mode auth is the default: the server sets HttpOnly access and refresh cookies on login, and reads them back on every request. In the browser, the cookie jar handles it automatically when you set credentials: 'include'. In a Server Component, there is no cookie jar — you have to read the request cookies with next/headers and forward them explicitly.

So far so standard. Here's the trap.

next/headers is a server-only module. If you import it from a file that's reachable by the client bundle, Next.js fails the build with a clear error. Fine, you think — I'll guard the import behind a runtime check:

if (typeof window === 'undefined') {
  const { cookies } = await import('next/headers');
  // ...
}

This does not work. The bundler statically resolves the import graph. The dynamic import() still counts as a reference. Build fails. You discover this the first time you try to use a "shared" HTTP client from a 'use client' component.

The fix that actually works is to expose two entry points:

src/lib/utils/http/
├── shared/                ← Universal foundation
├── fetch-client/          ← Fetch adapter
├── axios-client/          ← Axios adapter
├── __bundle-sentinel__/   ← Build-time tripwire (more on this in §5)
├── client-utils.ts        ← TokenRefreshManager
├── token-store.ts         ← secureStorageTokenStore
├── index.ts               ← Universal entry: '@/lib/utils/http'
└── server.ts              ← Server-only entry: '@/lib/utils/http/server'

The universal entry never touches next/headers. Safe to import from anywhere — client components, Server Components, Edge, isomorphic utils.

The server entry imports next/headers and wires up a cookieResolver that reads the request cookies on every call:

// src/lib/utils/http/server.ts
import 'server-only';
import { cookies } from 'next/headers';
// ...

async function readServerCookieHeader(): Promise<string | undefined> {
  const all = (await cookies()).getAll();
  if (all.length === 0) return undefined;
  return all.map((c) => `${c.name}=${c.value}`).join('; ');
}

export const fetchClient = createFetchClient({
  tokenStore: secureStorageTokenStore,
  onUnauthorized: handleUnauthorizedRedirect,
  cache: 'no-store',
  cookieResolver: readServerCookieHeader,
});

The 'server-only' import at the top is the kill switch: if a 'use client' file ever imports from @/lib/utils/http/server, the build fails with a clear error from the server-only package. The split is the entire design — you can't get it wrong because the type system and the bundler both enforce it.

Call sites become trivially correct:

// app/[locale]/profile/page.tsx (Server Component)
import { fetchClient } from '@/lib/utils/http/server';

export default async function ProfilePage() {
  const result = await fetchClient.get<User>('/auth/me');  // cookies forwarded
  if (result.isLeft()) return <SignedOut />;
  return <Profile user={result.value} />;
}

// any client component
'use client';
import { fetchClient } from '@/lib/utils/http';

export function Profile() {
  // Browser cookie jar carries the session cookie automatically.
  const result = await fetchClient.get<User>('/auth/me');
  // ...
}

Token refresh that doesn't thunder-herd

Every team I've worked on has, at some point, accidentally built a token-refresh path that fires N concurrent refresh requests when N concurrent calls hit a 401 at the same time. Then the server's refresh-rate-limiter trips and everyone gets logged out.

The fix is a small debounced manager. While a refresh is in flight, subsequent 401s wait in a queue:

// src/lib/utils/http/client-utils.ts
export class TokenRefreshManager {
  private state = { isRefreshing: false, queue: [], attempts: 0, lastAttempt: 0 };

  async handleRefresh(refreshFn: () => Promise<string | null>): Promise<string | null> {
    if (this.state.isRefreshing) {
      return new Promise((resolve) => this.state.queue.push(resolve));
    }

    const now = Date.now();
    if (now - this.state.lastAttempt < TOKEN_REFRESH_CONFIG.COOLDOWN_MS) {
      this.state.attempts++;
      if (this.state.attempts >= TOKEN_REFRESH_CONFIG.MAX_ATTEMPTS) {
        logger.error('Max refresh attempts reached. Stopping to prevent infinite loop.');
        this.state.attempts = 0;
        return null;
      }
    } else {
      this.state.attempts = 0;
    }
    this.state.lastAttempt = now;
    this.state.isRefreshing = true;

    const drainQueue = (token: string | null) => {
      const waiters = this.state.queue;
      this.state.queue = [];
      for (const resolve of waiters) resolve(token);
    };

    try {
      const token = await refreshFn();
      drainQueue(token);
      return token;
    } catch (err) {
      logger.error({ err }, 'Unexpected error in token refresh');
      drainQueue(null);
      return null;
    } finally {
      this.state.isRefreshing = false;
    }
  }
}

MAX_ATTEMPTS = 3 within COOLDOWN_MS = 1000. Past that, the manager clears local state and calls onUnauthorized() — defaulted to redirect to /login?redirectTo=<current>. Both clients share the same manager class. Both pass it the same refreshAuthToken function. The behavior is identical regardless of which client made the original call.

X-Request-Id correlation, end-to-end

Every outgoing request gets stamped with a fresh UUID matching ^[A-Za-z0-9_-]{1,128}$. A well-behaved server-side correlation layer echoes client-supplied IDs that match the pattern, generates its own otherwise, and stamps every response with X-Request-Id (both as a header and as a requestId field in error envelopes).

The client reads the value, stashes it on ApiException.requestId, and your error handler can log it:

const result = await fetchClient.get('/users/123');
if (result.isLeft()) {
  logger.error({ requestId: result.value.requestId }, 'lookup failed');
  // Now grep browser logs AND server logs for the same requestId.
}

The five minutes you spend correlating a production incident pays this back the first time it happens.

Typed queries and pagination, built in

The starter ships base query types for both offset- and cursor-based pagination:

export interface BaseQueryParams {
  page?: number;
  size?: number;
  search?: string;
  sort?: string;
  order?: 'asc' | 'desc';
}

export interface BaseCursorQueryParams {
  cursor?: string;
  size?: number;
  search?: string;
  sort?: string;
  order?: 'asc' | 'desc';
}

You extend these per endpoint:

interface UsersQuery extends BaseQueryParams {
  status?: 'active' | 'invited' | 'disabled';
  roleId?: string;
}

await fetchClient.get<PaginatedApiResponse<User>>('/users', {
  params: { page: 2, size: 20, status: 'active' } satisfies UsersQuery,
});

The shared toSearchParams serializer skips undefined/null/'' so server defaults stay implicit, and repeats array values for ?tag=a&tag=b style queries. Both clients use the same serializer — query strings are byte-identical regardless of which one made the call. (Axios's default serializer is replaced for exactly this reason.)

5. The build-time tripwire that catches the bug you can't reproduce

Here's the regression I was most afraid of: someone, six months from now, refactors a util in the universal HTTP entry. They innocently import a helper that, three transitive imports later, lands on next/headers. The build still passes — because the helper was only added to a code path that isn't reached by the bundler today. Six weeks later, someone uses that code path from a 'use client' file and prod breaks.

I wanted a tripwire that fails the build the moment the import graph is contaminated, regardless of whether anyone is using the contaminated path yet.

That's the __bundle-sentinel__ file:

// src/lib/utils/http/__bundle-sentinel__/client-bundle-sentinel.tsx
'use client';

import {
  axiosClient,
  createAxiosClient,
  createFetchClient,
  fetchClient,
  toSearchParams,
} from '@/lib/utils/http';

const __sentinel__ = {
  axiosClient,
  createAxiosClient,
  createFetchClient,
  fetchClient,
  toSearchParams,
};

export function HttpClientBundleSentinel(): null {
  if (typeof window !== 'undefined') {
    (window as unknown as { __http_sentinel__: unknown }).__http_sentinel__ = __sentinel__;
  }
  return null;
}

Three properties hold this together:

  1. The file is marked 'use client', so its entire transitive import graph must be valid for the client bundle.
  2. It imports every public symbol from @/lib/utils/http. If any of them ever pull a server-only module into the client graph, the build fails immediately.
  3. It's referenced from app/[locale]/layout.tsx, so the route tree pulls it into a real production build. Next.js prunes unreferenced files, so a dangling import wouldn't be a regression test.

The component renders null — its only purpose is to exist in the bundle graph. The window assignment exists so tree-shaking can't elide the import references.

It looks weird. It is weird. It's also the cheapest insurance I know how to write against a class of bugs that's expensive to debug in production. Don't delete it.

6. Either + ApiException: errors as values

The Either<L, R> type is a hand-rolled tagged union with Left and Right constructors:

export class Left<L> {
  readonly tag = 'left' as const;
  readonly value: L;

  isLeft(): this is Left<L> { return true; }
  isRight(): this is Right<never> { return false; }
  map<R>(_fn: (r: never) => R): Left<L> { return this; }
  mapLeft<NL>(fn: (l: L) => NL): Left<NL> { return Left.of(fn(this.value)); }
  fold<T>(onLeft: (l: L) => T, _onRight: (r: never) => T): T { return onLeft(this.value); }
}

export class Right<R> {
  readonly tag = 'right' as const;
  readonly value: R;

  isLeft(): this is Left<never> { return false; }
  isRight(): this is Right<R> { return true; }
  map<NR>(fn: (r: R) => NR): Right<NR> { return Right.of(fn(this.value)); }
  fold<T>(_onLeft: (l: never) => T, onRight: (r: R) => T): T { return onRight(this.value); }
}

export type Either<L, R> = Left<L> | Right<R>;

Three patterns at the call site, all valid:

const result = await fetchClient.get<User>('/users/123');

// 1. Guard + value
if (result.isLeft()) return handleError(result.value);
const user = result.value;

// 2. fold
const greeting = result.fold(
  (err) => `Error: ${err.message}`,
  (user) => `Hello, ${user.name}`,
);

// 3. isRight when you only care about the happy path
if (result.isRight()) setUser(result.value);

I went back and forth on whether to use a library (fp-ts, neverthrow, purify-ts). The reasons I landed on a hand-rolled version:

  • The starter is consumed by other projects via the @teispace/next-maker CLI. Every dep is a future "why do I have this in my bundle" question. A 70-line file with no transitive deps is easier to defend.
  • The surface I actually use is tiny: isLeft/isRight/value/map/mapLeft/fold. The libraries add a hundred other operators that are great for FP-curious teams and noise for everyone else.
  • It composes cleanly with ApiException, which is the only shape of error that ever lands on the left.

ApiException itself is opinionated. It exposes everything the API can plausibly send and adds form-friendly helpers:

export class ApiException extends Error {
  status: number;
  code?: string;
  errors?: Record<string, string>[];
  data?: Record<string, unknown>;
  path?: string;
  requestId?: string;

  containsKey(key: string): boolean { /* ... */ }
  getErrorMessage(key: string): string | undefined { /* ... */ }
  getErrorMessageIfExists(key: string): string { /* ... */ }
  getFieldErrors(): Record<string, string> { /* ... */ }
}

The one-liner for form validation is setFieldErrors(result.value.getFieldErrors()). That's the kind of API I want to write once and never think about again.

7. The WebSocket layer: same pattern, stricter rules

Real apps need WebSockets for at least three things: presence ("user X is online"), live updates ("a new message arrived"), and force-disconnect signals ("your session was revoked, sign out").

The WS layer mirrors the HTTP layer's design philosophy with one important difference: it throws on SSR misuse rather than silently no-op-ing.

// src/lib/utils/ws/shared/runtime.ts
export class WsSsrError extends Error {
  readonly code = WS_LOCAL_ERROR_CODES.SSR_BLOCKED;

  constructor(method: string) {
    super(
      `[ws] ${method}() was called in a server context. ` +
        `WebSocket clients run in the browser only. ` +
        `Move the call into a "use client" component, or guard it with typeof window !== 'undefined'.`,
    );
    this.name = 'WsSsrError';
  }
}

export function ensureBrowser(method: string): void {
  if (isServer()) throw new WsSsrError(method);
}

Opening a WebSocket from a Server Component is always a bug. Surfacing it immediately is far kinder than letting it reach production as "the socket mysteriously never connects."

Lazy connect, Proxy-backed singleton

The default wsClient is a Proxy that lazily constructs the underlying instance on the first method call:

let _wsClient: WsClient | null = null;

function getWsClient(): WsClient {
  if (!_wsClient) _wsClient = new WsClient();
  return _wsClient;
}

export const wsClient = new Proxy({} as WsClient, {
  get(_target, prop, receiver) {
    const client = getWsClient();
    const value = Reflect.get(client, prop, receiver);
    return typeof value === 'function' ? value.bind(client) : value;
  },
});

Why a Proxy? Because the WS module is sometimes imported by isomorphic files. With a normal singleton, instantiating at module load would trigger ensureBrowser() in places it shouldn't fire. The Proxy defers the instantiation until you actually call a method — by which time you're either in a 'use client' file or you've hit WsSsrError and you know exactly why.

The three hooks, and what lazy connect actually means 

useWsStatus()           // reads connection state from Redux
useWsEvent(name, fn)    // subscribes to a server event; lazy-connects on first call
useWsEmit()             // returns a typed emit function

The contract that makes this nice: feature code never calls wsClient.connect() explicitly. The first useWsEvent mount in the entire app triggers the connection. No subscribers means no socket — the transport doesn't open at module load just because you imported the module.

'use client';
import { useEffect } from 'react';
import { useWsEvent, useWsEmit, useWsStatus } from '@/lib/utils/ws';

export function PresenceWidget({ userId }: { userId: string }) {
  const { isConnected } = useWsStatus();
  const emit = useWsEmit();

  useEffect(() => {
    if (!isConnected) return;
    emit('presence:subscribe', { userId });
    return () => { emit('presence:unsubscribe', { userId }); };
  }, [isConnected, userId, emit]);

  useWsEvent('presence:online', ({ userId: uid }) => {
    if (uid === userId) console.log(`${userId} is online`);
  });

  return <span>{isConnected ? '🟢' : '⚪'}</span>;
}

Typed events via declaration merging

ClientToServerEvents and ServerToClientEvents are the contract:

export interface ClientToServerEvents {
  ping: (ack?: () => void) => void;
  'auth:token:renew': (
    payload: { refreshToken: string },
    ack?: (result: { success: boolean; error?: WsErrorPayload }) => void,
  ) => void;
  'presence:subscribe': (payload: { userId: string }) => void;
  'presence:unsubscribe': (payload: { userId: string }) => void;
}

export interface ServerToClientEvents {
  pong: (payload: WsPongPayload) => void;
  error: (payload: WsErrorPayload) => void;
  'auth:error': (payload: WsErrorPayload) => void;
  'auth:token:renewed': (payload: WsTokenRenewedPayload) => void;
  'auth:force:disconnect': (payload: WsForceDisconnectPayload) => void;
  'presence:online': (payload: WsPresencePayload) => void;
  'presence:offline': (payload: WsPresencePayload) => void;
  'presence:status': (payload: WsPresenceStatusPayload) => void;
}

Features extend them via TypeScript declaration merging:

// src/features/chat/types/ws-events.ts
import '@/lib/utils/ws';

declare module '@/lib/utils/ws' {
  interface ClientToServerEvents {
    'message:send': (payload: { roomId: string; content: string }) => void;
  }
  interface ServerToClientEvents {
    'message:new': (payload: {
      id: string;
      roomId: string;
      authorId: string;
      content: string;
      createdAt: string;
    }) => void;
  }
}

After that, emit('message:send', { roomId, content }) and useWsEvent('message:new', (msg) => ...) are both fully typed at the call site. No casts, no any.

auth:force:disconnect — branch on reconnectable, not reason

This is a contract I've seen teams get wrong twice. The server can disconnect a socket for many reasons (session revoked, max connections, rate limited, server shutting down, roles changed, max age). Some of those should auto-reconnect; some should not. The client must always branch on the reconnectable: boolean flag, never on the reason string.

const WS_DISCONNECT_REASON = {
  SESSION_REVOKED: 'session_revoked',     // reconnectable: false
  MAX_CONNECTIONS: 'max_connections',     // reconnectable: false
  RATE_LIMITED: 'rate_limited',           // reconnectable: false
  ROLES_CHANGED: 'roles_changed',         // reconnectable: true
  SERVER_SHUTDOWN: 'server_shutdown',     // reconnectable: true
  MAX_AGE: 'max_age',                     // reconnectable: true
} as const;

The reason is for logs and UX ("you were signed out because…"). The boolean is the contract: if it's false, the client sets a fatalDisconnect latch and disables reconnection on the underlying Manager. Reasons can be added or renamed server-side without coordinating a client release; the boolean is what your code branches on.

State flows through Redux, but only via the bridge

The wsClient has a typed lifecycle emitter (statusChange, error, forceDisconnect, socketIdChange, pong). attachWsBridge subscribes to those and dispatches into the ws Redux slice. The bridge is the only code path that ever dispatches WS slice actions. Feature code reads via selectors and never dispatches into this slice directly.

// src/lib/utils/ws/redux/bridge.ts
export function attachWsBridge(client: WsClient, dispatch: AppDispatch): () => void {
  const offStatus = client.on('statusChange', (status, socketId) => {
    dispatch(wsStatusChanged({ status, socketId }));
  });
  const offError = client.on('error', (payload) => dispatch(wsErrored(payload)));
  const offForce = client.on('forceDisconnect', ({ reason, reconnectable }) => {
    dispatch(wsForceDisconnected({ reason, reconnectable }));
  });
  // ...
  return () => { offStatus(); offError(); offForce(); /* ... */ };
}

The bridge is mounted once, from StoreProvider:

useEffect(() => {
  const store = storeRef.current;
  if (!store) return;
  return attachWsBridge(wsClient, store.dispatch);
}, []);

And critically — the ws slice is intentionally NOT wrapped in persistReducer:

// src/store/rootReducer.ts
export const rootReducer = combineReducers({
  count: persistReducer(countPersistConfig, countReducer),
  ws: wsReducer, // ephemeral — connection state across reloads is meaningless
});

Persisting "connected: true" would lie about the actual transport on first paint. The bridge dispatches the real status as soon as the WS client mounts. Don't add it to persistence.

8. Per-request Redux store with SSR-safe persistence

The default Redux setup tutorials configure the store at module top-level:

// DON'T do this in SSR
export const store = configureStore({ reducer });

This works for a SPA. It breaks for SSR: two concurrent requests share the same store instance, and one request's state can leak into another's render. You also can't pre-populate the store from a Server Component because the store was built at boot, before any request existed.

The fix is a fresh store per request, built inside the provider with useRef:

// src/providers/StoreProvider.tsx
'use client';
import { useEffect, useRef } from 'react';
import { Provider } from 'react-redux';
import type { Persistor } from 'redux-persist';
import { PersistGate } from 'redux-persist/integration/react';
import { attachWsBridge, wsClient } from '@/lib/utils/ws';
import { type AppState, type AppStore, makeStore } from '@/store';
import { createPersistor } from '@/store/persistor';

type StoreProviderProps = {
  children: React.ReactNode;
  preloadedState?: Partial<AppState>;
};

export const StoreProvider = ({ children, preloadedState }: StoreProviderProps) => {
  const storeRef = useRef<AppStore | null>(null);
  const persistorRef = useRef<Persistor | null>(null);

  if (!storeRef.current) {
    storeRef.current = makeStore(preloadedState);
    persistorRef.current = createPersistor(storeRef.current);
  }

  useEffect(() => {
    const store = storeRef.current;
    if (!store) return;
    return attachWsBridge(wsClient, store.dispatch);
  }, []);

  return (
    <Provider store={storeRef.current}>
      <PersistGate persistor={persistorRef.current as Persistor} loading={children}>
        {children}
      </PersistGate>
    </Provider>
  );
};

Three things to notice:

  1. useRef instead of useState. useState's lazy initializer would also work, but useRef is the convention for "make this once per mount, stable forever."
  2. makeStore(preloadedState) accepts an initial slice. A Server Component can fetch user/session data and pass it down to the store via RootProvider. The client store starts with that data already in place — no hydration round-trip, no loading flicker.
  3. PersistGate with loading={children} instead of loading={<Spinner />}. This is a non-blocking SSR pattern: the children render immediately with the in-memory state, and rehydrated state lands as soon as the persistor loads it. The alternative (showing a spinner during rehydrate) blanks the screen on every cold load and looks awful.

The SSR-safe storage adapter is the other piece. redux-persist's default localStorage adapter complains loudly when imported in a Node environment ("failed to create sync storage, falling back to noop"). The fix is a tiny shim:

// src/store/storage.ts
import type { WebStorage } from 'redux-persist';
import createWebStorage from 'redux-persist/lib/storage/createWebStorage';

const createNoopStorage = (): WebStorage => ({
  getItem: (_key) => Promise.resolve(null),
  setItem: (_key, _value) => Promise.resolve(),
  removeItem: (_key) => Promise.resolve(),
});

const storage: WebStorage =
  typeof window !== 'undefined' ? createWebStorage('local') : createNoopStorage();

export default storage;

Real localStorage in the browser, typed no-op on the server. The warning disappears and the typings stay honest.

Per-feature persist configs

A subtle convention: persistence config lives with the feature, not in a central place:

// src/features/counter/store/persist.ts
const COUNT_PERSIST_VERSION = 1;

const migrations = {
  // 2: (state) => ({ ...state, newField: defaultValue }),
} satisfies Record<number, (state: PersistedState) => PersistedState>;

export const countPersistConfig: PersistConfig<CounterState> = {
  key: 'count',
  storage,
  version: COUNT_PERSIST_VERSION,
  whitelist: ['value'],
  migrate: createMigrate(migrations, { debug: false }),
};

rootReducer.ts composes them:

export const rootReducer = combineReducers({
  count: persistReducer(countPersistConfig, countReducer),
  ws: wsReducer,
});

When a feature is deleted, its persistence config goes with it. When a feature's state shape changes, the migration is in the same folder as the slice. The cognitive overhead of "where's the persist config for X" drops to zero.

9. i18n with next-intl: static rendering that actually works

The starter uses next-intl with a [locale] route group. The setup is conventional, but two specific knobs make a meaningful difference.

localePrefix: 'never' in src/i18n/routing.ts keeps URLs free of the locale segment by default. This is the right default for most apps — users get /about instead of /en/about, the canonical SEO URL is clean, and you can flip it to 'always' or 'as-needed' if your locale strategy requires visible prefixes later.

getTimeZone() from the env keeps SSR deterministic:

// src/i18n/request.ts
export default getRequestConfig(async ({ requestLocale }) => {
  const requested = await requestLocale;
  const locale = hasLocale(routing.locales, requested) ? requested : routing.defaultLocale;

  return {
    locale,
    timeZone: env.DEFAULT_TIMEZONE,
    messages: (await import(`./translations/${locale}.json`)).default,
  };
});

Without an explicit timeZone, next-intl falls back to the environment's local time zone and logs an ENVIRONMENT_FALLBACK warning on every render. Worse, server and client may end up with different time zones, causing hydration mismatches on dates. Setting it explicitly silences the warning and keeps the SSR output deterministic.

The RootLayout reads both messages and time zone on the server, then passes them down through RootProvider:

const [messages, timeZone] = await Promise.all([getMessages(), getTimeZone()]);

return (
  <html lang={locale} dir={getLocaleDirection(locale)} suppressHydrationWarning>
    <body className={`${livvic.variable} bg-light antialiased dark:bg-dark`}>
      <RootProvider locale={locale} messages={messages} timeZone={timeZone}>
        <HttpClientBundleSentinel />
        {children}
      </RootProvider>
    </body>
  </html>
);

suppressHydrationWarning is on the <html> element because the theme provider toggles a class on it before React hydrates — the only legitimate case for that prop.

The locale list is data, in src/lib/config/app-locales.ts. The routing.ts config reads from it. Adding a locale is three or four edits (translation file, type widening, list update). The README walks through it.

10. Logger, secure storage, and the small things that compound

Logger

The default Node.js logger story is console.log. It's fine in dev. It's a disaster in production: no structure, no levels, no redaction, no log aggregator support.

The starter uses pino with environment-aware transport:

function buildServerLogger(): Logger {
  if (isTest) return pino({ ...baseOptions, level: LogLevel.SILENT });

  if (isProd) {
    return pino(baseOptions, pino.destination({ sync: false }));
  }

  return pino({
    ...baseOptions,
    transport: {
      target: 'pino-pretty',
      options: {
        colorize: true,
        singleLine: true,
        translateTime: 'yyyy-mm-dd HH:MM:ss.l',
        ignore: 'pid,hostname',
      },
    },
  });
}

Three behaviors:

  • test: silent. No IO, no worker threads. Keeps CI output clean.
  • dev: pino-pretty, single-line, colorized, with readable timestamps.
  • prod: raw JSON to stdout via pino.destination({ sync: false }). Async writes, no transport overhead, drops straight into Datadog/CloudWatch/etc.

Redaction paths are declared centrally:

export const SENSITIVE_KEYS = [
  'password', 'passwordConfirmation', 'token',
  'accessToken', 'refreshToken', 'secret', 'apiKey', 'creditCard',
];

export const SENSITIVE_HEADERS = ['authorization', 'cookie', 'set-cookie'];

export const SENSITIVE_REDACTION_PATHS = [
  ...SENSITIVE_KEYS.map((key) => `*.${key}`),
  ...SENSITIVE_HEADERS.map((header) => `req.headers["${header}"]`),
  ...SENSITIVE_KEYS.map((key) => `req.body.${key}`),
  ...SENSITIVE_KEYS.map((key) => `req.body.*.${key}`),
];

Anything that matches gets [REDACTED]. You can log a whole request object — including headers and body — without leaking tokens. The Biome noConsole rule errors on console.log so nobody accidentally bypasses the logger.

Secure storage

react-secure-storage is wrapped in src/services/storage/secure-storage.service.ts. The wrapper exists for two reasons:

  1. It centralizes the storage keys (access_token, refresh_token) so they aren't string-typed across the codebase.
  2. It wraps every read in a try/catch — the underlying library throws if its encryption fingerprint changes (e.g. after a browser data clear), and the right behavior is to return null, not crash.

In default cookie-mode (SAVE_AUTH_TOKENS = false), this whole wrapper is inert — the cookies are HttpOnly and never touch JS. Flip the constant and the bearer-token plumbing wakes up. No code changes needed.

The test setup stubs the library globally because react-secure-storage constructs an EncryptionService at module load that calls <canvas>.getContext for browser fingerprinting, and jsdom doesn't implement canvas:

// test/setup.ts
vi.mock('react-secure-storage', () => {
  const store = new Map<string, unknown>();
  return {
    default: {
      setItem: (k: string, v: unknown) => store.set(k, v),
      getItem: (k: string) => store.get(k) ?? null,
      removeItem: (k: string) => store.delete(k),
      clear: () => store.clear(),
    },
  };
});

vi.mock('server-only', () => ({}));

The server-only stub is necessary too: that package throws at module load outside a Next.js server bundle (the bundler is supposed to redirect it to a no-op). Vitest doesn't do that redirect, so we stub it manually for tests. Production builds are unaffected.

11. Quality gates: three Husky hooks, one CI workflow, a custom deprecated-API scanner

The hooks layer is what makes the day-90 defaults stick.

pre-commit:

yarn env:sync --check         # is .env.example in sync with .env?
yarn lint-staged              # Biome on staged files only
STAGED_TS_FILES=$(git diff --cached --name-only --diff-filter=ACMR | grep -E '\.(ts|tsx)$' || true)
[ -n "$STAGED_TS_FILES" ] && yarn type-check

Fast (under 5s most commits). Type-check is conditional on staged TS files. Lint-staged only touches changed files.

pre-push:

yarn ci:check                 # Biome lint + format + import sort (single pass)
yarn type-check
yarn check:deprecated
yarn test                     # Vitest, full run

Build is deliberately left to CI — pre-push should be fast enough that contributors don't try to --no-verify around it. Build takes 30-60s; lint + tests take 10-15s.

commit-msg: commitlint with @commitlint/config-conventional. yarn commit runs commitizen for a guided prompt if you want it.

CI runs the same five steps in sequence (ci:check → type-check → check:deprecated → test → build). Single job, same Node version as local development, cached yarn.

The most novel piece is check:deprecated. TypeScript flags @deprecated usage at the "suggestion" severity level, which means tsc --noEmit happily passes a codebase full of deprecated API calls. Biome doesn't catch this either. So the starter ships a small compiler-API script that walks every identifier and fails if any resolved symbol carries the @deprecated tag:

// scripts/check-deprecated.ts
import ts from 'typescript';
import path from 'node:path';

const cwd = process.cwd();
const configPath = ts.findConfigFile(cwd, ts.sys.fileExists, 'tsconfig.json');
const raw = ts.readConfigFile(configPath!, ts.sys.readFile).config;
const parsed = ts.parseJsonConfigFileContent(raw, ts.sys, path.dirname(configPath!));

const program = ts.createProgram({ rootNames: parsed.fileNames, options: parsed.options });
const checker = program.getTypeChecker();

function isDeprecated(sym: ts.Symbol | undefined): boolean {
  if (!sym) return false;
  return sym.getJsDocTags(checker).some((tag) => tag.name === 'deprecated');
}

let hits = 0;
for (const sourceFile of program.getSourceFiles()) {
  if (sourceFile.fileName.includes('node_modules')) continue;
  if (!sourceFile.fileName.startsWith(cwd)) continue;

  const visit = (node: ts.Node): void => {
    if (ts.isIdentifier(node)) {
      const sym = checker.getSymbolAtLocation(node);
      if (isDeprecated(sym)) {
        const { line, character } = sourceFile.getLineAndCharacterOfPosition(node.getStart());
        console.log(
          `${path.relative(cwd, sourceFile.fileName)}:${line + 1}:${character + 1}  ${node.text}  (@deprecated)`,
        );
        hits++;
      }
    }
    ts.forEachChild(node, visit);
  };
  visit(sourceFile);
}

process.exit(hits === 0 ? 0 : 1);

About 50 lines. Runs in ~3s on a project of this size. Catches every deprecated React API, every deprecated Next API, every deprecated method in your own code with /** @deprecated */ on it. Wired into validate, pre-push, and CI.

This is the kind of script you write once and forget about; six months later it pays for itself by flagging the deprecation you didn't see in the release notes.

12. What I deliberately left out

Just as important as what's in the starter is what isn't. Restraint is the harder discipline.

  • No auth feature. Only the contract types (AuthUser, AuthTokens, AuthResponse, RefreshTokensResponse) and the endpoint paths (AppApis.auth.*). The CHANGELOG notes that empty features/auth/, features/dashboard/, app/[locale]/auth/, and services/api/ directories existed in an earlier version and were deleted: "they had no real code and were drifting away from what the docs described." Empty scaffolding rots fast — better to have a clean slate.
  • No shared UI components. components/index.ts is empty. There's no Button, no Input, no Card. Bring your own design system; the starter shouldn't impose one.
  • No form library. Pick TanStack Form, React Hook Form, or native FormData. The HTTP layer's getFieldErrors() integrates with any of them.
  • No data-fetching cache. No SWR, no TanStack Query. The HTTP clients return raw ResultAsync<T>. Caching is a downstream choice, and the wrong default here costs you a lot of bundle.
  • No analytics, no error tracking. ApiException.requestId is the hook point for Sentry/Datadog/etc. — wire in what you use.
  • No payment, email, file upload. Pure transport + state + i18n shell.

The model is: the template provides the frame; features ship separately. This is what the @teispace/next-maker CLI is for — it composes the template with feature packs to generate end products. The split keeps the template stable across many projects.

13. Lessons that generalize beyond this starter

Stepping back from the specific code, four principles shaped almost every decision:

1. Encode boundaries in the type system or the build, not in convention.

The universal/server HTTP entry split would have been "be careful where you import from" as a convention. As a structural split with 'server-only' and a bundle sentinel, it's a compile-time error if you get it wrong. Conventions degrade as teams grow; type-level and build-level enforcement does not.

2. Fail fast at the boundary; trust internal invariants.

Env vars validated at module load. WS connect throws on SSR. HTTP returns Either instead of throwing. The pattern is the same: catch the bad case where it enters the system, surface it loudly, and let the rest of the code assume things are well-formed.

3. Make the day-1 defaults match the day-90 needs.

Pre-request Redux store, PersistGate with loading={children}, env-aware logger transport, X-Request-Id correlation, sensitive-key redaction. None of these matter on day 1. All of them matter the first time you ship to production and start debugging. Bake them in early; the marginal cost on day 1 is zero, and the savings on day 90 are real.

4. The cost of one wrong default compounds across every project that copies the template.

This is why the starter is unusually opinionated about things like "no console.log" or "always log the requestId on failures." A template gets copied into N projects. A bad default in the template becomes N projects with the same bad default. Holding the line on small things — single quotes, no ESLint, never process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_* directly — pays off N times over.

Try it

If any of this resonated:

  • The starter repo: github.com/teispace/nextjs-starter
  • The CLI that scaffolds applications from it: @teispace/next-maker
  • The theme package referenced throughout: @teispace/next-themes

Clone it. Read the comments — the codebase practices what it preaches about "comments explain WHY, not WHAT," and the rationale for every non-obvious choice is in the code where the choice was made.

If you find a design decision you disagree with, open an issue. Half the value of writing this article is having my own assumptions stress-tested by people who've hit different production traps than I have.

If you found this useful, follow me for more deep-dives on production Next.js, TypeScript, and the boring infrastructure choices that make or break a project.
